title: Compact angle spectra and classification
subtitle: G2 lecture 051000 · expanded mathematical companion
adaptation: Standalone companion adapted from the source spoken lecture and display-only mathematics appendix. Explicit hypotheses, stepwise proofs, worked examples, and local vector diagrams; no narration edits.

slides.title: When does an angle list classify a pair?
slides.lead: Two ordered pairs of subspaces can be compared up to a unitary change of coordinates.
body: In finite dimensions, the four elementary intersection dimensions and the principal angles with multiplicities describe the complete relative geometry. In infinite dimensions, a numerical angle list is sufficient only under additional spectral hypotheses.
Compactness lets a positive cosine operator be reconstructed from discrete eigenvalues. Continuous spectral components require a richer unitary-equivalence invariant.
slides.takeaway: Classification needs endpoint dimensions plus the full generic cosine geometry.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 051000 · When does an angle list classify a pair?

slides.title: First record the four exact intersection spaces
slides.lead: The Halmos decomposition isolates the parts where two projections agree or disagree completely.
body: The spaces U∩V, U∩V⊥, U⊥∩V, and U⊥∩V⊥ are invariant under both projections, with each projection acting by zero or identity.
A unitary carrying one ordered pair to another must carry each corresponding intersection space onto its counterpart. Therefore their Hilbert-space dimensions are unavoidable classification data.
slides.mathtex: U\cap V,\quad U\cap V^\perp,\quad U^\perp\cap V,\quad U^\perp\cap V^\perp
slides.takeaway: The four endpoint spaces are discrete invariants of every ordered subspace pair.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 051000 · First record the four exact intersection spaces

slides.title: The generic cosine-square operator
slides.lead: Remove the four elementary pieces and study the remaining generic block.
body: On the U-half of this block the compression A=P_U P_V P_U is positive and bounded by the identity. A principal direction with angle θ gives eigenvalue cos² θ.
A describes how strongly U-vectors survive projection into V. Its unitary-equivalence class determines the remaining geometry through the cosine–sine reconstruction.
slides.takeaway: Generic principal-angle data live in a positive contraction, not merely a list of numbers.

slides.title: Compactness changes what spectral data can do
slides.lead: A positive compact operator has an orthonormal basis for the closure of its range made from eigenvectors.
body: Each nonzero eigenvalue has finite multiplicity, and if there are infinitely many distinct positive eigenvalues, they can accumulate only at zero.
Thus the multiset of nonzero eigenvalues, including multiplicities, determines a positive compact operator up to unitary equivalence once its zero eigenspace is also accounted for.
slides.takeaway: Compact positive operators admit complete discrete spectral descriptions.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 051000 · Compactness changes what spectral data can do

slides.title: What the angle multiplicities record
slides.lead: If cos² θ occurs on a three-dimensional eigenspace, the angle θ has multiplicity three.
body: Counting an eigenvalue only once loses the number of independent principal planes carrying that angle. Classification must match the dimension of each nonzero eigenspace.
On the generic Halmos block, exact zero and one eigenvectors have been removed as endpoint pieces. Zero can still occur as a spectral accumulation point without being an eigenvalue.
slides.takeaway: The spectrum must be counted with multiplicity, and spectral limits are not new defect vectors.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 051000 · What the angle multiplicities record

slides.title: An infinite diagonal example
slides.lead: On ℓ²(N), set Ce_n=(n+2)^{-1}e_n, and define S=(I−C²)^{1/2}.
body: In the doubled Hilbert space, let U be the first copy and V consist of pairs (Cx,Sx). Each coordinate gives a principal plane with cosine 1/(n+2).
The cosine-square operator C² is compact because its diagonal values tend to zero. No angle equals ninety degrees, but the angles approach that limit. The projection gap is still one.
slides.takeaway: A compact angle spectrum can approach a right angle without an exact crossed defect.

slides.title: A multiplication operator with no eigenvectors
slides.lead: On L²(0,1), define C by (Cf)(t)=t f(t), then S by multiplication with √(1−t²).
body: The doubled-space construction U={(f,0)} and V={(Cf,Sf)} again gives two closed subspaces with a meaningful angle geometry.
But C has no nonzero eigenvectors: an eigenvector at λ would be supported at the single point t=λ, a measure-zero set. The spectrum is [0,1], so an eigenvalue list misses the geometry entirely.
slides.takeaway: Continuous-spectrum geometry cannot be classified by point-eigenvalue multiplicities.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 051000 · A multiplication operator with no eigenvectors

slides.title: Compact-pair classification theorem
slides.lead: Assume for each ordered pair that the ambient triple projection P_U P_V P_U is compact.
body: Then the generic cosine block is compact. Two ordered pairs are unitarily equivalent exactly when their four elementary intersection spaces are isometrically equivalent and the generic nonzero cosine-square eigenspaces have the same dimensions at each eigenvalue.
The ambient compactness assumption is important. Without it one must retain the full operator-equivalence class of the generic cosine contraction, including continuous spectrum.
slides.takeaway: With compactness, endpoint multiplicities plus the generic angle multiplicities classify the pair.

slides.title: Why the classification theorem works
slides.lead: Necessity follows because an ambient intertwining unitary preserves every projection polynomial and every Halmos intersection.
body: It therefore preserves the spectrum and eigenspace dimensions of the generic cosine block. For sufficiency, choose matching isometries on the four elementary spaces.

The compact positive spectral theorem matches eigenbases on the generic source halves. The cosine–sine block construction then extends those matches to the generic complement halves, assembling a unitary of the ambient spaces.
slides.takeaway: Match elementary spaces directly and generic pieces by the compact spectral theorem.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 051000 · Why the classification theorem works

slides.title: Do not confuse a limit with a defect
slides.lead: A right-angle defect is a nonzero vector annihilated by the generic cosine, while a limiting right angle need not produce one.
body: In the diagonal example every cosine is strictly positive, so the generic cosine is injective even though its spectrum contains zero as an accumulation point.

In the multiplication example zero is again in the spectrum but not an eigenvalue. The two examples show why classification must distinguish exact kernel dimensions, discrete multiplicities, and continuous spectral behavior.
slides.takeaway: An angle limit belongs to the spectrum, but need not correspond to any principal vector.
